newsitem.title: USA: Lagging international markets offer opportunities.
newsitem.headline: Lagging international markets offer opportunities.

text.p: Investors who discovered international funds during the past decade haven't had much to smile about lately.

Many investors bought their first shares in international funds during the late 1980s, when foreign markets were delivering very strong returns. But since then, the U.S. market has pulled ahead of foreign markets, and during the past few years the gap has widened sharply. Since 1992, international funds as a group have returned 9.1 percent annually, compared with a 13.1 percent annual return for domestic stock funds.

As a result, some investors in international stock funds may be ready to bring their money back home. But they might get better results if they hold on to their overseas funds. In fact, if you haven't yet invested in an international stock fund, this might be a good time to do so.

The relatively poor performance of international funds in recent years is due partly to the terrible performance of the Japanese stock market, which has been plagued by that country's economic, political and financial troubles. Many other foreign economies have experienced sluggish economic growth and relatively high interest rates. Meanwhile, the U.S. economy has enjoyed falling interest rates and solid economic growth.

Such conditions aren't likely to endure forever. It's quite possible that struggling economies abroad will deliver much better results during the years ahead -- and our economy could run into a few potholes.

Moreover, foreign markets' relative underperformance means that many stocks of overseas companies are trading at bargain prices. Those stocks will have further to rise in the event of good news. By contrast, U.S. stock prices reflect investors' optimism that conditions will remain positive for financial assets. If that viewpoint changes, U.S. stocks could decline quite a long way.
International funds also increase the diversification of your portfolio. That's because foreign stock markets don't move in lockstep with each other or with our market over the long-term.

Example: A recent study by InterSec for mutual fund sponsor T. Rowe Price found that from 1980 through 1996, U.S. and foreign markets as a group moved together only about 22 percent of the time. Some markets had an even lower correlation with the U.S. stock market. For example, prices of Japanese stocks and U.S. stocks moved together only 6 percent of the time.
Conclusion: You can sharply reduce the volatility of your portfolio by investing in more than one country's stock market.

That said, it's hard for an individual investor to compile a portfolio of foreign shares. Many of the shares that offer the best opportunities aren't easy for individuals to purchase directly. What's more, it can be difficult to find a broker who is familiar with overseas markets or accounting rules that can obscure the real value of a foreign company's stock.

Thus, mutual funds are probably the best way for most individual investors to put money to work in foreign markets. But picking the right fund can be tricky. International stock funds come in a variety of flavors, including funds that specialise in a particular region or country; funds that invest only in emerging markets; and funds that stick to established markets such as the markets of Western Europe and Japan. Some funds specialise in shares of small, fast-growing overseas companies, while others stick to well-established blue chips.

What fund is right for you? If you're making your first overseas investment, stick to a well-established, broadly diversified fund such as Hotchkis & Wiley International (800-346-7301; $5,000 minimum investment; no load). Managers Sarah Ketterer and Harry Hartford favour large companies in developed overseas markets such as the United Kingdom and Japan. The fund's returns have been 95 percent higher than its typical competitor during the past five years, with about 20 percent less volatility.

Another solid entry is T. Rowe Price International Stock (800-638-5660; $2,500 minimum; no load), one of only a few international funds that has existed since the early 1980's. It has gained 10.1 percent annually during the past 10 years, versus 7.8 percent for the average foreign stock fund.

Later, you may decide to take on more risk by adding a fund that has a bigger stake in emerging markets or small company shares. Consider Founders Passport (800-525-2440; $1,000 minimum; no load), which focuses on shares of rapidly-growing small firms, or Oakmark International (800-625-6275; $2,500 minimum; no load). The fund recently held around 38 percent of its portfolio in stocks issued by companies in countries such as Argentina and Malaysia.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
